# Sacubitril/Valsartan in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence and Therapeutic Integration

**Introduction and Mechanism of Action**
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden with high morbidity and mortality. For decades, therapeutic strategies focused on suppressing the overactive renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and sympathetic nervous system. However, the introduction of angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) marked a paradigm shift in cardiovascular medicine [1,13]. Sacubitril/valsartan, the first-in-class ARNI, combines the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril with the angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) valsartan [13]. Neprilysin degrades various endogenous vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin. By inhibiting neprilysin, sacubitril enhances vasodilation, natriuresis, and diuresis, while inhibiting fibrosis and hypertrophy. However, because neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II, simultaneous blockade of the angiotensin II type 1 ($\text{AT}_1$) receptor via valsartan is mandatory [13]. Previous attempts to combine a neprilysin inhibitor with an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor (e.g., omapatrilat) were abandoned due to an unacceptable risk of serious angioedema [16].

**Clinical Evidence in HFrEF**
The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established sacubitril/valsartan as a foundational therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [1]. In this double-blind trial of 8,442 patients with LVEF $\le$ 40%, sacubitril/valsartan (200 mg twice daily) reduced the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20% compared to enalapril (10 mg twice daily), alongside a 16% reduction in all-cause mortality [1]. Subsequent analyses of PARADIGM-HF demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan delayed clinical progression [7], reduced sudden cardiac death [27], improved health-related quality of life [22], and slowed HbA1c progression in patients with diabetes [23]. To optimize clinical implementation, the TITRATION study confirmed that a conservative 6-week uptitration regimen was safe and well-tolerated [14], while further analysis supported that even lower-than-target doses of sacubitril/valsartan conferred superior clinical benefit compared to enalapril [17].

**In-Hospital Initiation and Acute Heart Failure**
Initiating sacubitril/valsartan during or immediately after hospitalization for acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) has been extensively evaluated. The PIONEER-HF trial randomized 881 patients hospitalized for ADHF to receive sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril once hemodynamically stabilized [3]. Sacubitril/valsartan led to a significantly greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels and a significant reduction in the exploratory endpoint of rehospitalization for HF [3,19]. The TRANSITION study supported these findings, demonstrating that initiating sacubitril/valsartan either in-hospital or shortly after discharge was highly feasible and safe [4]. In contrast, the LIFE trial evaluated sacubitril/valsartan in patients with advanced HFrEF (NYHA class IV) and did not show a statistically significant difference in NT-proBNP reduction or clinical outcomes compared to valsartan alone, highlighting potential limits of benefit in end-stage refractory HF [18].

**Reverse Remodeling and Mechanistic Insights**
The clinical benefits of sacubitril/valsartan are closely linked to favorable cardiac remodeling. The prospective PROVE-HF trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan therapy was associated with significant reductions in NT-proBNP, which strongly correlated with improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular end-diastolic volume index, and left atrial volume index over 12 months [5]. The EVALUATE-HF trial further evaluated hemodynamics, showing a significant reduction in left ventricular end-diastolic volume compared to enalapril [6]. Additionally, the PRIME trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced functional mitral regurgitation, offering another mechanistic explanation for its clinical efficacy [25].

**Expanding Across the Ejection Fraction Spectrum**
Following its success in HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan was investigated in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). After promising phase II data from the PARAMOUNT trial [15], the large-scale PARAGON-HF trial randomized 4,822 patients with LVEF $\ge$ 45% to sacubitril/valsartan or valsartan [2]. Although sacubitril/valsartan narrowly missed statistical significance for the primary composite endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death (p=0.059), subgroup analyses suggested heterogeneity of treatment effect, with notable benefit observed in patients with LVEF below the median (approx. $\le$ 57%) and in women [2]. A pooled analysis of the PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF trials confirmed that the clinical benefits of sacubitril/valsartan extend into the mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) range, up to an LVEF of approximately 55-60% [9]. In the acute setting, the PARAGLIDE-HF trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced NT-proBNP in stabilized patients with stabilized HFmrEF and HFpEF compared to valsartan, further validating its use in broader HF populations [20].

**Safety, Renal Protection, and Tolerability**
The safety profile of sacubitril/valsartan is favorable, though distinct from ACE inhibitors. Symptomatic hypotension is more common with sacubitril/valsartan, whereas hyperkalemia, renal impairment, and cough are less frequent [1,7]. ARNI therapy has demonstrated consistent renal protection. In both HFrEF and HFpEF cohorts, sacubitril/valsartan preserved estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and slowed renal decline compared to enalapril or valsartan [8,24], a benefit also observed in patients with chronic kidney disease in the UK HARP-III trial [21]. Concerns regarding potential cognitive impairment due to accumulation of amyloid-beta peptides in the brain were definitively addressed by the PERSPECTIVE trial, which showed no adverse effects on cognitive function over a 3-year follow-up period [26]. Furthermore, sacubitril/valsartan has been associated with a reduction in ventricular arrhythmias [29]. While the PARADISE-MI trial did not demonstrate a significant reduction in cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization following acute myocardial infarction compared to ramipril, the overall safety was confirmed [12].

**Guideline Recommendations and Economic Value**
Based on this robust body of evidence, current major guidelines have elevated sacubitril/valsartan to a Class I recommendation (first-line therapy) for patients with HFrEF [10,11,30]. Guidelines also recommend sacubitril/valsartan in patients with HFmrEF and select patients with HFpEF, particularly those in the lower range of preserved LVEF [10,30]. Beyond clinical efficacy, health economic evaluations, such as those by Gaziano et al., have shown that sacubitril/valsartan is highly cost-effective compared to traditional ACE inhibitor therapy, driven by the significant reduction in costly hospital admissions [28].

**Conclusion**
Sacubitril/valsartan has transformed the management of heart failure. By simultaneously blocking the RAAS and enhancing natriuretic peptides, it achieves superior clinical outcomes, reverses adverse cardiac remodeling, and maintains a highly acceptable safety profile. Its utilization across the ejection fraction spectrum represents a major therapeutic milestone, offering a robust, guideline-directed foundation for improving survival and quality of life in patients suffering from heart failure.
